cues.text: Welcome to the Structural Organisation identification workshop.
Use several tissue clues together.
Typical parenchyma consists of living cells with relatively thin primary walls
and can support storage, photosynthesis or other metabolic roles.
Collenchyma provides flexible support and has living cells with unevenly
thickened walls, often conspicuous at the corners in the textbook example.
Mature sclerenchyma cells typically have thick lignified walls and are dead at
functional maturity.
A thick wall alone is not enough to identify every cell: note its
distribution,
material and the cell's living state.
These are standard comparisons, not a claim that one tiny or poorly preserved
section always gives a complete identification.
Meristems are identified by both their position and their contribution to
growth.
Apical meristems at root and shoot tips support primary growth in length.
Lateral meristems, such as vascular cambium in a typical woody stem,
contribute
to increased girth.
Intercalary meristems occur between more mature regions, with familiar
examples
near the bases of grass leaves or internodes.
Do not identify a meristem only because a plant is getting larger: specify the
location and the kind of growth being measured.
Permanent tissues have differentiated roles, although some plant cells can
regain division capacity under suitable circumstances.
A positional classification and a functional observation should support each
other.
Xylem and phloem are complex tissues because each contains different cell
types
working together.
Mature vessel elements and tracheids are generally dead conducting elements of
xylem, but xylem parenchyma is living.
It is therefore incorrect to say that every xylem cell is dead.
In angiosperms, sieve tube elements and companion cells are important phloem
components.
Sieve tube elements are living but lack a nucleus at functional maturity and
depend on associated cellular support.
Xylem is strongly associated with water and mineral transport, while phloem
moves organic assimilates between sources and sinks.
Those functions do not erase the structural differences among the cells within
each tissue.
In the standard school comparison, roots often show xylem and phloem arranged
on different radii, called radial vascular bundles.
Stem bundles commonly have xylem and phloem together on the same radius,
called
conjoint bundles.
Exarch xylem in a typical root places the earlier formed protoxylem toward the
outside, while endarch xylem in a typical stem places protoxylem toward the
centre.
A typical dicot stem shows bundles in a ring, whereas a typical monocot stem
has scattered bundles.
These are comparative textbook patterns with biological exceptions.
Use the organ, bundle arrangement and maturation direction together instead of
calling every circular section a root.
A typical dorsiventral dicot leaf has palisade mesophyll toward the upper
surface and spongy mesophyll with larger intercellular spaces toward the lower
surface.
This organisation supports photosynthesis and internal gas movement.
Many such leaves have more stomata on the lower surface, but that pattern is
not universal for all leaves.
Isobilateral leaves show a different comparative organisation, and aquatic
leaves can have their own adaptations.
The stomatal pore is bounded by guard cells; it is not an empty gap between
arbitrary epidermal cells.
Read the leaf type and labelled surfaces before assigning palisade position or
making a claim about where every stoma must occur.
A specimen's position and function do not always reveal its organ origin.
A potato tuber grows underground and stores food, yet it is a modified stem.
Its eyes are associated with buds at nodes, which provide important structural
evidence.
A ginger rhizome is another underground stem example.
By contrast, a storage root remains a root despite sharing a storage role.
Do not classify every underground organ as a root or every swollen organ as a
fruit.
In an identification question, look for nodes, internodes, buds and the stated
developmental origin.
Similar functions can arise in different organs, so function alone is not a
sufficient key.
Animal tissue identification begins with arrangement as well as cell shape.
Epithelium forms closely packed sheets covering surfaces or lining spaces.
Simple epithelium has one layer, while stratified epithelium has multiple
layers.
Thin simple squamous epithelium is suited to exchange at familiar sites such
as
alveoli, whereas multiple layers can provide protection from abrasion.
Connective tissues typically have cells distributed within a more prominent
extracellular matrix.
Blood is a connective tissue with plasma as its fluid matrix, so connective
tissue need not be a solid sheet or a rigid structure.
Do not identify every tissue solely from whether its cells look round in one
section.
Striations alone do not distinguish skeletal from cardiac muscle because
both show them.
In the standard comparison, skeletal fibres are long, cylindrical and
multinucleate.
Cardiac fibres are branched, typically have central nuclei, and connect
through
intercalated discs.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped and lack the visible striations of the
other two types.
Their usual control patterns also differ, but a photograph does not directly
show voluntary control.
Use a combination of shape, nuclei, branching, junctions and striation rather
than a single feature.
Section orientation and image quality can hide a clue, so an unlabelled
specimen may require several observations before identification is secure.
